Fruit flies usually come from ripe or rotting produce, damp drains, or fermenting liquids. Here's how to get rid of them:

**Remove the source first.** Check fruit bowls, onions, potatoes, and anything overripe. Toss or refrigerate what's rotting. Wipe up spilled juice, soda, and sticky residue.

**Clean drains.** Pour boiling water down sink drains, then scrub the drain opening and disposal rubber gaskets. Fruit flies often breed in the gunk there.

**Set a trap.** Put a few inches of apple cider vinegar or wine in a jar, add a drop of dish soap, and cover the top with plastic wrap. Poke small holes in the wrap. The flies get in but can't get out.

**Keep things covered.** Store fruit in the fridge, and keep trash cans sealed and emptied often.

Most infestations clear up within a week or two once the breeding source is gone. If they keep coming back, look for hidden sources like a forgotten compost bin, recycling, or a drain you haven't cleaned.

The best way to learn chess as an adult is to combine three habits.

First, learn the basics well: how each piece moves, special rules like castling and en passant, and simple checkmate patterns. Use a free course like Chess.com's lessons or Lichess Learn.

Second, play regularly with a time control of 10 to 15 minutes per side. Games teach you more than almost anything else, and online platforms match you with opponents of similar strength.

Third, review your games. After each one, look for the moment the game turned, then use an engine like Stockfish to check your mistakes. Focus on recurring errors, such as leaving pieces undefended or missing opponent threats.

Solve tactics puzzles daily for 15 to 20 minutes. Pattern recognition improves quickly this way.

Finally, be patient. Adults often progress faster than they expect, but steady practice matters more than long, occasional sessions. Consider a coach or a local club once you're comfortable, since in-person play and feedback can accelerate improvement.

Puppy biting is normal, since puppies explore the world with their mouths and are teething. Here's what tends to work:

**Redirect to a toy.** When your puppy mouths you, calmly swap your hand or clothing for a chew toy. Praise them when they bite the toy.

**Say "ouch" and pause.** Say a firm "ouch" or "no bite" in a calm voice, then stop playing for 20 to 30 seconds. Puppies learn that biting makes fun end.

**Don't use hands as toys.** Avoid wiggling fingers or roughhousing with your hands, since this teaches them that hands are for biting.

**Tire them out.** A tired puppy bites less. Provide daily walks, play sessions, and short training games.

**Offer plenty of chew options.** Frozen carrots, rubber chews, and teething toys help with sore gums.

**Be consistent.** Everyone in the household should respond the same way.

Most puppies grow out of biting by about 6 months. If it persists or becomes aggressive, consult a certified trainer or your veterinarian.

Fixing an old phone is often the smarter choice, especially if the problem is small. Start by checking the cause. A dying battery can usually be replaced for well under the cost of a new phone. A cracked screen is also a common, affordable repair. Before paying for anything, try a few free fixes: back up your data, do a software update, clear storage, close background apps, and reset the phone if it's sluggish.

Buy a new phone if the device no longer receives security updates, since unpatched phones are a real risk. Also consider replacing it if it has frequent crashes, water damage, or a repair cost above roughly half the price of a comparable new or refurbished model. Apps may also stop working on old hardware over time.

If you do upgrade, a certified refurbished phone often gives you good value with a warranty. Whichever you choose, get a quote from a reputable repair shop first so you can compare costs with confidence.

Basil is tropical and hates cold, dry air, so give it these basics:

**Light:** Place it in your sunniest window, ideally south- or west-facing. Basil needs 6 or more hours of direct light a day. If you don't have that, use a full-spectrum LED grow light 6 to 12 inches above the plant for 12 to 14 hours daily.

**Water:** Keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy. Water when the top half-inch feels dry, and always use a pot with drainage holes.

**Temperature:** Keep it between 65 and 80°F (18 to 27°C). Keep it away from cold drafts, doors, and heating vents.

**Harvest often:** Pinch off the top sets of leaves just above a pair of leaves. This keeps the plant bushy and delays flowering. Pinch off any flower buds as soon as they appear.

**Feed lightly:** Use a diluted liquid fertilizer every 2 to 4 weeks during active growth.

**Humidity:** Mist occasionally or group it with other plants if your air is very dry.

With good light and regular trimming, your basil should keep producing for months.

Frequent deadline changes are frustrating, but you can often manage them. Start by asking your boss for clarity: "Just to confirm, is this the new deadline, and what should I deprioritize to hit it?" This makes the tradeoff visible without sounding resistant.

Next, keep a simple written record. When a deadline shifts, send a short follow-up such as "Confirming the project is now due Friday instead of Wednesday." That creates a reference point and helps if priorities get questioned later.

If changes are constant, look for patterns. Are they driven by a specific client, a particular leader, or unclear goals? Raising this in a one-on-one can help: "I want to deliver well on these. Could we agree on how urgent changes get communicated, so I can plan better?"

Finally, protect your capacity. Avoid absorbing every shift silently, since that often leads to burnout. If the pattern continues despite your efforts, talk with your manager's manager or HR about workload and planning.

Focus on your audience rather than your fear. Make eye contact, speak to one person at a time, and remember they want you to succeed. Pausing is powerful, so don't rush to fill silences.

Get feedback. Join a group like Toastmasters, where you'll get regular, supportive critiques in a low-pressure setting.

Java apps often look like they use too much memory because the JVM reserves far more than it actively needs. Several things can cause this:

1. **Heap sizing:** The JVM grows the heap up to `-Xmx` (or 1/4 of physical RAM by default) and rarely shrinks it. Garbage that hasn't been collected yet still counts toward usage.

2. **Non-heap memory:** Metaspace (class metadata), thread stacks (about 1 MB per thread), code cache (JIT output), and direct buffers all sit outside the heap. Libraries that generate classes at runtime, such as Spring, Hibernate, or Groovy, can push Metaspace very high.

3. **Container limits:** In Docker or Kubernetes, older JVMs may ignore cgroup limits. Use `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` (default in modern JDKs) or set `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`.

4. **Memory leaks:** Static collections, unclosed resources, listeners that are never removed, or caches with no eviction policy keep objects reachable.

**To diagnose:**
- Run `jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary` (start the JVM with `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`).
- Use `jmap -histo:live <pid>` to find the biggest object types.
- Take a heap dump with `jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>` and analyze it in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM.
- Watch GC behavior with `-Xlog:gc*`.

If the heap plateaus after GC, the usage is probably just sizing. If it keeps climbing, look for a leak. Share your JVM flags and the output of `jcmd ... VM.native_memory` for more specific help.

Use `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. It removes the commit but leaves your changes staged, so they're ready to recommit.

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1
```

If you want the changes unstaged instead, use mixed mode, which is the default:

```bash
git reset HEAD~1
```

Either way, your working-tree files stay exactly as they were.

To make changes to the commit message or contents instead of just undoing it, use:

```bash
git commit --amend
```

Avoid `git reset --hard HEAD~1` unless you want to discard the changes too.

If you've already pushed the commit, rewriting history will require a force push, so coordinate with anyone else working on the branch first. A safer alternative for shared branches is `git revert HEAD`, which creates a new commit that undoes the previous one.

A **mutex** (mutual exclusion lock) allows only one thread to access a resource at a time. It has an ownership concept: only the thread that locked it can unlock it. Its purpose is protecting a critical section, so that shared data is never modified by two threads at once.

A **semaphore** is a counter-based signaling mechanism. It allows up to N threads to access a resource concurrently, where N is the initial count. Threads call `wait()` (or `P`/`acquire`) to decrement the count and block if it's zero, and `signal()` (or `V`/`release`) to increment it. Any thread can signal, not just the one that waited, so semaphores work well for coordination between threads or processes, such as producer-consumer queues or limiting a connection pool.

Key differences:

- **Ownership:** Mutexes have an owner; semaphores don't.
- **Count:** Mutexes are binary (locked or unlocked); semaphores are integer counters.
- **Use case:** Mutexes provide mutual exclusion; semaphores provide signaling and resource counting.

A binary semaphore (count of 1) looks like a mutex, but it lacks ownership, so it isn't a substitute. Use a mutex to protect data, and a semaphore to signal events or limit concurrency.

Slowdowns under load usually come from a few common bottlenecks. Start by measuring:

1. **Find the bottleneck.** Check CPU, memory, and I/O on the server during load. Use APM tools or profilers (py-spy, async-profiler, pprof) to see where time goes.

2. **Database queries.** This is the most common cause. Look for N+1 queries, missing indexes, and `SELECT *` on large tables. Enable slow query logs and run `EXPLAIN` on suspect queries.

3. **Connection pool exhaustion.** If requests wait for DB connections, latency spikes. Size the pool to match your DB's capacity, not your request concurrency.

4. **Blocking calls.** Synchronous HTTP calls to other services, file I/O, or CPU-heavy work inside request handlers tie up workers. Move them to async tasks or queues.

5. **No caching.** Cache expensive, rarely changing responses with Redis or HTTP caching headers (`Cache-Control`, `ETag`).

6. **Unbounded responses.** Endpoints returning thousands of rows without pagination slow down under load. Add pagination and limit payload size.

7. **Too few workers.** Check that your app server (gunicorn, uvicorn, Node cluster, etc.) has enough workers for the cores available.

8. **Missing timeouts and retries.** Slow downstream services can cascade. Set timeouts and circuit breakers.

# On-Call Handover

This page describes how on-call responsibility passes from one engineer to the next. A good handover keeps incidents from falling through the cracks, avoids repeating investigations, and makes sure the incoming engineer starts with the context they need.

## Scope

This process applies to every engineer on a primary or secondary on-call rotation. It covers handovers at the end of each shift, handovers when someone goes off rotation mid-week, and handovers to a backup who is covering unexpectedly.

## Roles

- **Outgoing on-call:** The engineer currently holding the pager. Responsible for writing the handover summary and walking through open items.
- **Incoming on-call:** The engineer taking over the pager. Responsible for reading the handover, asking questions, and confirming they have taken over.
- **Shift lead (if applicable):** Resolves disagreements about priority and confirms that the handover happened.

## When Handover Happens

- At the scheduled rotation time, typically Monday 10:00 local time for weekly rotations.
- Early, if the outgoing engineer is unwell, traveling, or otherwise unable to cover. In that case, notify the shift lead and the incoming engineer as soon as possible.
- At the end of a major incident that spans the rotation boundary. The incident commander should coordinate the handover, not just the on-call engineer.

## Before the Handover

The outgoing engineer should prepare the following at least 30 minutes before the rotation change:

1. **Update the handover doc.** Use the template below and copy it into the on-call log for the current rotation.
2. **Review open alerts and tickets.** Close anything resolved. For anything still open, note its current state and next step.
3. **Check silences and maintenance windows.** List any active silences, scheduled changes, or deploys that may fire alerts during the next shift.
4. **Review recent pages.** Note any alert that fired repeatedly, was acknowledged without action, or was a false positive. Flag alerts that need tuning.
5. **Confirm access.** Make sure the incoming engineer has access to the pager app, dashboards, runbooks, and any production tooling they may need.

## Handover Template

```
## On-call handover: [Outgoing] → [Incoming]
Date/time: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM [timezone]

### Active incidents
- [Incident ID / link]: status, impact, current action, next step, who to contact

### Open tickets or investigations
- [Ticket link]: summary, current hypothesis, blocker if any

### Recent pages (last shift)
- [Alert name] × [count]: outcome (resolved / false positive / needs follow-up)

### Scheduled changes in the next shift
- [Deploy / maintenance / migration]: time, owner, rollback plan

### Silences and suppressions
- [Alert or service]: reason, expiry

### Things to watch
- Known flaky alerts, services under elevated load, customer escalations pending

### Notes
- Anything else the incoming engineer should know
```

## During the Handover

The handover should be a short live conversation, 10 to 15 minutes, followed by written confirmation.

1. The outgoing engineer walks through the handover document, starting with active incidents.
2. The incoming engineer asks questions. Questions are expected and should not be treated as criticism.
3. Both engineers confirm which open items transfer to the incoming engineer. Items not explicitly transferred remain with the outgoing engineer until they confirm otherwise.
4. The incoming engineer verifies they can receive pages by sending a test notification or checking the paging app.

## Confirming the Handover

The handover is complete when:

- The incoming engineer has acknowledged in the on-call channel: "Taking over on-call from [name]."
- The paging system shows the incoming engineer as primary.
- The outgoing engineer has posted a link to the handover doc in the on-call channel.

Until these three things happen, the outgoing engineer remains responsible for pages.

## After the Handover

- The outgoing engineer remains reachable for at least 24 hours for questions about their shift, unless they are off work.
- The incoming engineer owns all new pages and any transferred items.
- Any item the incoming engineer cannot resolve should be escalated to the shift lead, not left for the outgoing engineer to pick up informally.

## Common Problems

- **Missing context:** The most frequent issue is an incident that was in progress but not mentioned. Prevention: check the incident channel and open tickets during preparation, not from memory.
- **Silent transfers:** Work that was assumed to be handed over but never confirmed. Prevention: transfer items by name in the live conversation.
- **Alert fatigue carried forward:** Noisy alerts that everyone knows to ignore but nobody fixes. Prevention: flag them in the handover and file a tuning ticket.
- **Handover skipped under pressure:** Usually during a live incident. Prevention: the incident commander decides when a handover can be deferred, and the reason is recorded.

# Feature Flag System

Feature flags let us turn functionality on or off at runtime without deploying new code. Each flag is a named switch, such as `new-checkout-flow`, that the application checks before running a given code path. Flags let us ship code behind a switch, test it in production with a small group of users, gradually roll it out, and disable it instantly if something breaks.

**How it works:**
- **Define:** Create a flag in the flag management service with a unique name, a description, and a default value.
- **Check:** In code, evaluate the flag (for example, `if flags.isEnabled("new-checkout-flow", user)`) and branch accordingly.
- **Target:** Rules decide who sees the feature, based on user ID, account, region, or percentage of traffic.
- **Clean up:** Once a feature is fully rolled out, remove the flag check and delete the flag. Stale flags add complexity.

**Guidelines:**
- Keep flag checks close to the entry point of a feature, not scattered through the codebase.
- Make sure the code works with the flag both on and off.
- Treat flags as temporary. Name them clearly and set an owner and removal date.
- Don't put secrets or sensitive configuration in flags.

Okay so. Feature flags. You'll hear about them constantly, so here's the short version before I forget what I was going to say.

They're just if-statements that live outside the code. Wrap a new thing in a flag, deploy it, and it's off until someone flips it on in the dashboard. That's the whole trick. Ship dark, turn on for 5% of users, watch the graphs, go to 100%, or yell and turn it off. No redeploy. Mostly.

A few things that will bite you:

- The flag service is a dependency now. If it's down, we fall back to the default value in code, so always check what that default is before you assume something's on.
- Flags pile up. Every flag you add is a branch someone has to remember to delete. Delete your flag after it's fully rolled out. Nobody does this. Be the exception. There's a ticket on the board about the 40 old ones and it's not getting better on its own.
- Don't put secrets or per-user permissions in flags. Those belong in the auth system. Flags are for "is this feature ready," not "is this person allowed."
- Test both sides. If you only test with the flag on, the flag-off path is a surprise waiting for a Tuesday night.
- Flag names are permanent-ish. Pick something that says what it does, not `new_checkout_v2_final_FINAL`.

If you're stuck, ask in the platform channel. Someone who has been here longer than me will know which flag is secretly load-bearing.

Drawing trained my eyes to slow down, and I found myself paying more attention to the ordinary world again.

- **Keep it short.** Fifteen minutes is easier to start than an afternoon.
- **Draw what's in front of you.** You don't need a perfect subject.
- **Don't erase the bad ones.** Flipping back through the pages shows how far you've come.
- **Expect discomfort.** The awkward phase is part of the process.

My first job was sorting donated produce. Bruised apples went one way, good oranges another, and anything questionable into the compost bin. It sounds simple, but I quickly learned how much food gets thrown away before it ever reaches a family. Our team rescued pallets of perfectly edible carrots that a grocery store had nearly tossed.

Later, I worked the pantry line, bagging groceries for families who came through in a steady stream. Many were parents with young kids. Some were seniors on fixed incomes. A few were people who had never imagined needing help until life pulled the rug out from under them. Nearly everyone said thank you, and a few shared small stories that stayed with me long after I drove home.

What struck me most was how ordinary it all was. The volunteers weren't saints. They were retirees, teenagers fulfilling service hours, nurses on day off, and neighbors who simply wanted to help. Together, they kept the shelves stocked.

If you've been thinking about volunteering but feel unsure, here's my advice: just show up. You don't need special skills, only a few free hours and a willingness to work alongside strangers. I'm already signed up for next month, and I suspect I'll leave with a full heart again.

# Does Social Media Do More Harm Than Good to Teenagers?

Social media has become a central part of adolescent life. Platforms promise connection, creativity, and information, yet critics link them to rising anxiety, depression, and disrupted sleep. Whether they do more harm than good depends on how we weigh these outcomes and which teenagers we consider. The evidence suggests that social media is neither pure poison nor pure benefit. Its effects are more harmful for some young people, particularly through heavy use and addictive design, and more beneficial for others.

The case for harm is substantial. Researchers such as Jean Twenge have documented correlations between heavy social media use and the rise in teen depression since the early 2010s. Features like infinite scrolling, algorithmic feeds, and visible like counts encourage compulsive checking. Cyberbullying follows students beyond the school day, and constant exposure to curated images can damage self-esteem, especially among girls. Many teenagers report losing sleep to late-night scrolling, and sleep loss itself worsens mood and concentration.

Yet dismissing social media entirely ignores real benefits. For LGBTQ teenagers, rural adolescents, and those with rare medical conditions, online communities can offer acceptance and support unavailable locally. Platforms let young people share creative work, learn new skills, and access news and educational material. Many teens use social media to maintain friendships, which can strengthen social bonds. Researchers like Amy Orben have cautioned that the average effects of social media on well-being are often small, and that how teens use these platforms may matter more than how much time they spend on them.

Ultimately, social media does more harm than good for some teenagers and more good than harm for others. The more useful question is whether these platforms are designed and used responsibly. Stronger privacy protections, age-appropriate design standards, digital literacy education, and open family conversations about intentional use could tilt the balance toward benefit. Until then, the most defensible conclusion is that social media's harms are concentrated among vulnerable and heavy users, while its benefits are more widely shared. That distinction makes a blanket verdict unwise.

Should Cities Ban Cars from Their Centres?

City centres are the heart of urban life, yet they are often choked by traffic, dominated by parked vehicles, and hostile to pedestrians. Banning cars from these areas offers a bold answer to these problems, and the case for it is strong.

The most compelling argument concerns health and safety. Vehicle emissions are a major source of air pollution, linked to asthma, heart disease, and premature death. Traffic collisions also kill and injure thousands of pedestrians and cyclists every year. Removing cars from dense districts would reduce both risks, protecting the people who live, work, and shop there.

Car-free zones also make economic and social sense. Pedestrianised streets have repeatedly boosted footfall for local businesses, and cities such as Copenhagen and Barcelona have shown that reclaiming road space for people creates lively public squares, cafes, and markets. Less space is needed for parking, freeing land for housing, parks, and community use.

Critics raise serious objections. Disabled residents, the elderly, and delivery drivers may depend on cars, and a ban could isolate them or harm small businesses that rely on passing trade. Some argue that bans simply push traffic and parking into surrounding neighbourhoods, shifting the burden rather than solving it. These concerns deserve real answers, not dismissal.

A middle path can address them. Cities can exempt residents with disabilities, permit deliveries during set hours, and invest heavily in public transport, cycling routes, and accessible alternatives before or alongside a ban. Phased implementation and consultation with local businesses can build support and allow adjustments.

On balance, cities should ban most private cars from their centres, paired with strong public transport and carefully designed exemptions. The benefits to health, safety, and urban vitality are substantial, and the problems critics identify can be managed through thoughtful planning rather than used as reasons to preserve the status quo.

Should cities ban cars from their centres? I used to think the answer was obviously yes, mostly because I hate circling the block in Bologna looking for a spot that doesn't exist. But the more I read about this, the less sure I am, and the messy parts are the interesting bit.

The case for a ban is pretty strong. Pontevedra in Galicia pedestrianised most of its old town in the late 1990s, and by most accounts its traffic deaths dropped and people started actually sitting in the squares. Ghent did something similar around its medieval core, and the cafés didn't die, which is what everyone had predicted. Cars also take up absurd amounts of space for what they do. A row of parked cars holds maybe a dozen people's worth of metal, sitting still for 23 hours a day.

But a ban isn't really a ban on cars. It's a ban on the car you own sitting outside your flat. Who gets hurt? Plumbers with tools, the old man on the fourth floor walk-up who can't carry a fridge up the stairs, deliveries, the family whose kid needs to get to the hospital at 2 a.m. Paris has been doing a version of this, and the reaction from taxi drivers and shopkeepers in the Marais was loud. Some of them had a point about footfall, even if the numbers are contested.

Then there's the question of where the traffic goes. Push it all to the ring road and you've made the outer districts worse, and those are usually where poorer people live. London's congestion charge cut traffic in the centre, but the evidence on whether it helped the outer boroughs is mixed. I went looking for a clean answer and didn't find one.

So my view, for what it's worth, is yes to most of it, but sequence it. Get the trams, buses and bike lanes running first, then close the streets, and exempt the people who genuinely need a car. A flat ban on day one feels like a fight the city will lose. A phased one, with the boring infrastructure already in place, seems much more likely to stick.

Should Schools Teach Personal Finance?

Every year, millions of students graduate with diplomas but little understanding of how to manage the money they will earn. They may know the causes of the Civil War or how to solve quadratic equations, yet they cannot explain how compound interest works, how a credit score is calculated, or why a retirement account matters. Schools should require personal finance education because financial decisions shape nearly every adult's life, and the classroom is the most equitable place to build that knowledge.

The stakes are high. Young adults face decisions about student loans, credit cards, car purchases, housing, and investing, often with no guidance beyond what their families happen to know. Families with financial expertise can pass that knowledge down, but many families cannot. A required course levels the playing field, ensuring that a student's future does not depend entirely on the money habits of the household they were born into.

Critics argue that schools are already overloaded and that financial literacy belongs at home. Yet many parents struggle with the same concepts, and time spent at home is not guaranteed to produce lessons. Others worry that adding a course means removing something else. This concern is legitimate, but personal finance can be woven into math classes through lessons on percentages, interest, and budgeting, so it does not require sacrificing core content.

Research on the effects of financial education is mixed, and some studies find that the benefits fade over time unless lessons are practical and timely. This is an argument for better design, not for abandoning the subject. Courses that teach students to build a real budget, compare loan offers, and understand paychecks and taxes tend to produce more lasting results than abstract lectures.

Ultimately, schools exist to prepare students for adult life. Few skills matter more to that life than the ability to manage money wisely. A thoughtfully designed personal finance requirement would give every student the tools to make informed choices, avoid costly mistakes, and build security for the future. Schools should teach it.

My sophomore year I took a required life skills class that was supposed to cover budgeting, taxes, and credit. We spent three weeks on the stock market, which I still don't really understand, and one afternoon on a worksheet about balancing a checkbook that nobody has used since maybe 1998. Our teacher, Mr. Feeney, kept apologizing for it. He wasn't a bad teacher. The curriculum just wanted us to learn everything in one semester.

I think schools should teach personal finance, but not the way most of them do, and that's the part people skip when they argue about it.

The case for it is pretty obvious to me. My cousin signed up for a store card at a Target register to get 15 percent off that day's purchase, then paid close to 30 percent interest for two years because nobody had explained what APR meant. My uncle still thinks his 401(k) is a savings account. Most people learn this stuff by getting burned, and the burn is expensive. If one semester keeps somebody from one bad car loan, that's worth a few weeks of class time.

The counterargument has teeth, though. Teachers are already stretched thin. Every year someone proposes a new required course, and something else gets cut, usually music or the one elective that was actually fun. And personal finance depends so much on circumstance. A kid whose parents talk about mortgages at dinner gets a different education than a kid whose mom is working two jobs and hiding the bills. A worksheet can't fix that, and a lot of the people pushing these mandates seem to think it can.

Still, I'd rather have the required class than not. Skip the stock market unit, or at least make it about not putting rent money into anything with a dog on the logo. Teach the boring stuff: how compound interest works against you on a balance, what a credit score actually measures, why an emergency fund matters more than you think at nineteen. Keep it short, keep it required, and pair it with something real, like every student opening an actual bank account before they graduate.

**Is Space Exploration Worth the Money?**

Every year, governments spend billions of dollars looking outward, and every year someone asks whether that money would do more good on Earth. The question deserves a serious answer, and I believe the answer is yes, space exploration is worth the cost.

The most obvious objection is that poverty, disease, and climate change are urgent, and space programs divert resources from them. This argument has force. Yet budgets for space are small compared with other government spending. NASA's annual budget is well under one percent of U.S. federal spending. Choosing to fund a telescope does not usually mean choosing against a hospital. Moreover, many of the problems space programs address are themselves Earth problems. Satellites track hurricanes, measure rising sea levels, monitor deforestation, and guide farmers in planting decisions. Climate science depends heavily on data gathered from orbit.

Space research has also produced practical technologies that reach ordinary life. Water purification systems, improved medical imaging, scratch-resistant lenses, and GPS navigation all trace back in part to work done for spaceflight. Such benefits are often unpredictable, which is precisely why basic exploration matters. Nobody knew that studying distant light would lead to better cancer detection, or that a navigation system built for missiles would one day guide delivery drivers.

Beyond practical returns, exploration answers fundamental questions. Are we alone? How did the solar system form? Could life exist on Europa or Mars? Discoveries like the thousands of exoplanets found in recent decades have transformed our understanding of our place in the universe. Human curiosity has always driven progress, and space is the frontier that tests it most.

Finally, space programs create something harder to measure: international cooperation and inspiration. The International Space Station has operated for decades with partners who might otherwise have little reason to work together. Students who watch a rover land on Mars often pursue careers in science and engineering.

Space exploration is not free, and it should face scrutiny. But its costs are modest, its benefits are real, and its promise is profound. A society that stops looking up risks losing both its knowledge and its ambition.

Should Students Be Paid for Good Grades?

This is a question that a lot of people have thought about, and I think there are good reasons on both sides. On one hand, grades are supposed to measure how much a student has learned, and if we pay for them, we might be giving money for something that isn't really the point of school. On the other hand, a lot of students work really hard and get good grades, and it seems unfair that they don't get anything for it.

The main argument for paying students is that it would motivate them. Some kids don't see a reason to try in school, especially if the subject seems boring or hard. If they knew that a good grade meant money, they might push themselves harder. It could also help students from poorer families who have to work part-time jobs and don't have as much time to study. Getting paid could take some of that pressure off.

But there are problems with this idea. If students are only working for money, they might stop caring about actually learning the material. They might cheat more often, or just memorize things for a test and forget them right after. Also, paying for grades could make school feel like a business instead of a place to grow. Teachers might also feel pressure to give higher grades so that the school doesn't have to pay out as much money.

Another problem is that not everyone starts at the same level. Some students have tutors, quiet homes, and parents who help them, so it might be easier for them to earn money. That might make the gap between rich and poor students even bigger.

In my opinion, paying students for grades is not a good idea. School should be about learning for its own sake. Instead of paying for grades, schools should find other ways to motivate students, like better teaching, more interesting classes, and support for students who are struggling. Money might work in the short term, but it probably wouldn't create people who love learning.

Should Students Be Paid for Good Grades?

Grades are supposed to measure learning, yet many students experience them as a currency. Paying students for good grades would make that currency literal. Although the idea is tempting as a motivator, it would do more harm than good.

The strongest argument for payment is that it rewards effort. Students from struggling schools or unstable homes often work harder for less reward, and a cash incentive could recognize that persistence. Financial pressure also pushes many students toward part-time jobs that eat into study time. If grades earned money, some students might find studying more worthwhile than working.

However, paying for grades would shift the purpose of education from understanding to earning. Students would learn to ask, "Will this be on the test?" rather than "Why does this matter?" Curiosity, which often leads to the deepest learning, rarely survives when every lesson carries a price tag. Research on extrinsic rewards, including studies by psychologists such as Edward Deci, suggests that external payment can reduce intrinsic motivation over time.

Payment would also distort honesty. When money depends on a grade, the temptation to cheat, pressure teachers to inflate scores, and encourage students to avoid difficult courses all increase. A student who takes an easy class to protect a paycheck is making a rational choice that undermines their own education.

Finally, the system would be unfair in a different way. Students with more natural ability or better preparation would earn more, while those who need the most help would have the least to gain. Paying for grades might reward advantage rather than effort.

A better approach would support students directly. Schools can offer tutoring, flexible schedules, and financial aid that reduces the need for work, all without tying money to a letter on a transcript. These measures address the real barriers students face while keeping grades focused on what they are meant to represent: learning.

The letter from the solicitor arrived on a Tuesday, between a catalogue for orthopaedic shoes and a notice about the bins. Nell read it standing at the kitchen counter, then read it again sitting down, as though posture might change what it said. It didn't. Her aunt Vivienne was dead. The Marlowe Picture House, all four hundred and twelve seats of it, was now hers.

She had not set foot in the place in nineteen years.

"You'll sell it," her husband said that evening, not unkindly, already reaching for the calculator app on his phone. "Thirty grand, maybe forty if the roof's sound. Then we finally fix the boiler."

Nell said nothing. She was thinking about the smell of the lobby, popcorn and damp velvet and the faint sweetness of the projector's cooling oil. She was thinking about Vivienne's hands, always cold, always ink-stained, pressing a ticket stub into Nell's palm at age seven and saying, *Everything you'll ever need to know about people is in who comes back for the second show.*

The next morning Nell drove across the county in the rain. The Marlowe sat at the end of Church Street, its green awning faded to the colour of old limes, its marquee letters missing so that it advertised only *ARL WE* and then, improbably, *OPEN*. Someone had written the second word by hand in white paint, and the paint was new.

She stood on the pavement with the key heavy in her coat pocket and looked up at the sign. Behind her, a bus sighed to a stop.

The key turned stiffly. Inside, the air was cold and still, and it held the faint, unmistakable scent of someone who had been sweeping recently.

Nell stepped into the dark, and the doors closed softly behind her.

The gate at the end of Marion's driveway still sticks in the same place, and she still has to lift it with her hip to make it swing. She noticed this the first morning she was back, standing in her dressing gown with a mug going cold in her hand, watching the wrought iron scrape its old groove in the gravel. Twenty years, and some things had simply decided not to change.

The house next door was different. The hedge that had once separated the two gardens had been cut down to a neat row of knee-high stumps, and in its place stood a fence of pale, new timber that someone had stained a color Marion would have called optimistic. Beyond it, a child's bicycle lay on its side in the grass, its pink bell catching the light.

She had come back to sort out her mother's things. That was the reason she gave the solicitor, the estate agent, and the woman at the corner shop who had asked, kindly, whether she was "one of the Hallorans." Marion had said yes, she supposed she was, and had not explained that she had grown up here, had left at nineteen with a single suitcase and a vow, and had sent Christmas cards to her mother every year that were never once returned with anything but a short, dutiful reply.

She had not expected to see Ruth Ashdown again. Ruth had been the reason for the vow, though neither of them had ever said so out loud. There had been a summer, a argument at the bottom of the garden, a word spoken that could not be taken back, and then two decades of silence conducted across a shared fence line.

The kettle clicked off inside. Marion turned to go back in, and that was when she heard the back door of the other house open.

The gate at the end of the lane had always stuck, and Margaret Dunphy had never once managed to lift it without swearing. She heard it groan now, and then she heard the careful, deliberate click of it being lowered again, which meant her neighbour had seen her coming and had decided to wait.

Harold Pike stood on the other side of the fence line with a rake in both hands, the way a man holds a rifle he has no intention of using. His hair had gone white. So had hers, though she had stopped noticing hers years ago, the way you stop noticing a stain on a sofa you have always owned.

Twenty years. Neither of them had kept an exact count, but they both knew the number. It had begun over a dead oak tree that came down in a storm and landed across both properties, and over who should pay to have it cut away, and over a few sharp words said in the road that had hardened into a silence neither one wanted to be first to break.

The wind moved through the poplars along the boundary. Somewhere behind her, a car door shut, and a dog barked twice and gave up.

Margaret had rehearsed this moment in the kitchen that morning, standing at the sink with her coffee going cold. She had planned a greeting, something light about the weather. Now, looking at his face, which was older and more tired than she had let herself imagine, the rehearsed words seemed ridiculous, like a speech for a funeral of someone neither of them had truly liked.

She set her hand on the top bar of the gate.

"Your tomatoes," she said finally. "They're still coming up over the wall, you know. Every August."

Harold's shoulders moved, something between a laugh and a breath caught too long.

"I know," he said. "I've been meaning to do something about that."

The last bus left the depot at 12:40, and Marisol was the only passenger who had stepped aboard it on purpose.

The driver didn't look up from his newspaper when the doors folded shut behind her. He just tapped the fare reader with two fingers, the way you'd greet someone you'd known for years, and the machine chirped its small, forgiving note. The interior lights hummed. Half of them were dead, so the bus moved through a series of dim islands, each one swallowing her for a few seconds before releasing her into the dark.

She chose the seat near the back, the one with the torn vinyl that had been patched with silver tape. Nobody had ever argued with her about it. Over the years she had learned that the seat you chose on the last bus said more about you than anything you might tell a stranger.

Outside, the city was closing its eyes. Shutters rolled down over bakeries and phone repair shops. A single neon sign buzzed its way through the word PHARMACY, and then the window slid past it and the word was gone. Rain had started somewhere around the stadium and now ran in thin, slanted lines across the glass, bending the streetlights into long amber smears.

The bus lurched onto the viaduct. Below, the rail yards stretched out in rows of shadowed freight cars, silent as sleeping animals.

Marisol pulled her coat tighter and reached into the pocket where the envelope still sat, its corner soft from handling. She had read the letter four times since Tuesday. She did not need to read it again. But her fingers kept finding it anyway, the way a tongue keeps finding a chipped tooth.

Across the aisle, an old man was asleep with his chin on his chest, a paper grocery bag wedged between his shoes. Two rows ahead, a young couple shared earbuds, their heads tilted together, laughing at something neither of them said aloud.

The driver turned a corner too quickly, and the bag at the old man's feet slid an inch toward the aisle.

Marisol watched it settle, and she thought, not for the first time that week, that everything was about to change.

The first thing Teodor noticed was that the perch was still moving its gills, which meant it had been dead for only a minute, maybe two. He had been standing on the wet planks of the pier since before sunrise, bored and cold, when his line gave a hard tug and then went slack. He hauled it in expecting a weed or a boot. Instead, a fat yellow-bellied perch came flopping over the rail, and when his grandfather's bait knife slit its belly open, something hard clicked against the blade.

He held it up to the gray light. A key. Small, brass, the color of old pennies, with a bow shaped like a clover and teeth worn smooth at the tips.

"Gross," said his sister Maren from the bench behind him, not looking up from her book. "Throw it back."

"It's a key."

"It's a fish guts key."

He rinsed it in the bucket of seawater, and the brass came up bright, almost warm, as if it had been lying in the sun instead of the belly of a fish. He turned it over. Stamped into the shank were letters so faint he had to tilt it toward the sky to read them: *H.V.* and beneath those, a small carved anchor.

Their grandfather had kept a locked tin box on the top shelf of the boathouse for as long as Teodor could remember. Nobody ever said what was inside. Every summer someone asked, and every summer Grandfather only smiled and said, "When it's time."

Teodor looked at the perch, then at the key, then at the long gray line of the boathouse roof at the end of the pier.

He wrapped the key in his handkerchief and put it in his pocket, where it sat heavy and cold against his leg for the rest of the morning, pressing reminders into him with every step he took toward the water's edge.

**The Interpreter's Small Mercies**

Marguerite had interpreted for the Ministry of Labor for nineteen years, and in all that time no one had ever caught her lying. She considered this the quiet achievement of her life.

The room smelled of radiator dust and wet wool. Across the steel table sat Mr. Oduya, a welder from Lagos with a bandaged thumb, and beside him a clerk named Hendricks, who had not looked up from his tablet since the hearing began. Hendricks wanted to know why Oduya had left his last position. Oduya answered in the careful Yoruba of a man who had rehearsed in the bathroom mirror. His supervisor had docked his pay for a missed shift, the shift he missed because his daughter was in the hospital with pneumonia.

Marguerite felt the familiar hinge in her chest, the small place where words turned.

"He says he was careless," she said in English. "He says it won't happen again."

Oduya's eyes flicked to her face. He did not know enough English to catch the lie, but he knew faces, and something in hers made him go still.

Hendricks typed. "Good. Ask him about the injury."

She asked. Oduya, thinking he had been asked whether the thumb had healed, answered at length: the hot iron, the foreman who had sworn at him in front of the crew, the hour he had spent in a parking lot afterward because he could not make himself drive home and tell his wife the rent was late again.

Marguerite translated perhaps a third of it. "He says the thumb is healing."

It was not the first time she had done this, and she told herself it was not the worst. Interpreters chose words all day long. Every sentence was a decision about what to carry across and what to leave on the riverbank. She had simply decided, long ago, that the riverbank was where cruelty belonged, and that a man's shame should not be typed into a file that would follow him for the rest of his life.

Hendricks sighed and tapped a key. "Fine. Tell him we'll need the supervisor's statement."

Marguerite turned to Oduya and, in Yoruba, said the thing she had not been asked to say. *Keep your head down. You did nothing wrong. Your daughter is well.*

He blinked, and for the first time that morning, he nodded.

Marisol had been translating the same letter for three days, and by the third afternoon she knew she was going to lie.

The letter came from Tomás Reyes, a fisherman in a coastal town she had never visited, written in a looping hand that slanted uphill. His daughter, Inés, had left for the city eleven years ago. Now the old man was dying, and he wanted her to come home. The letter said so in plain Spanish, without apology or fuss. *Ven a casa, mija. Ya no tengo fuerzas para esperar.*

Come home, my girl. I no longer have the strength to wait.

Marisol typed the sentence into the document and stopped. The cursor blinked. Outside her apartment window, a delivery truck backed up with a long, rising beep, and somewhere below, a dog barked at it.

The agency paid by the page. It paid well, which was why she had taken the job, and why she could not afford to lose it. But the agency also expected accuracy, and accuracy was the one thing she had decided to abandon.

She had her reasons. Inés Reyes was the client's sister, or so the cover note said. The client was a law firm in Houston handling an inheritance dispute over a boat, a strip of waterfront, and a bank account nobody wanted to split. Marisol had read enough of the file to see what would happen if the old man's words arrived in English exactly as written. The sentence would become evidence. Evidence of abandonment. Evidence of a father who had waited, and of a daughter who had not come.

So she would soften it. Not much. Just enough.

She deleted *Ya no tengo fuerzas* and typed something else. Her hands were steady. That surprised her.

RIVERSIDE, Ohio - The bronze eagle statue that once stood at the entrance of Riverside Park is back where it belongs, nearly two years after it was stolen in the early hours of a December morning.

Police announced Tuesday that the 300-pound sculpture was recovered from a storage unit on the outskirts of town. Detectives say a tip from a local scrap dealer led them to the unit, where the statue had been hidden under a tarp among stacked lumber and old appliances.

"We never gave up on this case, and neither did the community," said Detective Maria Lopez. "Residents kept asking about the eagle, and that pressure helped keep our investigators focused."

The statue, created in 1958 by local sculptor Harold Brenner, was a gift to the city from the Riverside Historical Society. It was removed from its granite pedestal sometime between midnight and dawn, leaving only bolts behind. Its disappearance prompted a community fundraising drive that raised $12,000 for restoration.

Two suspects, both 34-year-old men from the county, have been charged with theft and criminal damage. Their names have not been released pending arraignment.

Parks Director Janet Morrow said the eagle will undergo a full inspection before being reinstalled. Minor damage to one wing is expected, though officials say the piece is largely intact.

A rededication ceremony is scheduled for Saturday at 10 a.m. at the park's main gate. Mayor Thomas Reed is expected to speak, and the Historical Society will unveil a new plaque honoring Brenner's work.

"It's a good day for Riverside," Reed said. "This eagle has been watching over our park for more than sixty years, and we're glad to have it watching again."

I hope you're kinder to yourself than I've been lately. I hope you've learned that rest isn't something you earn after finishing everything, and that the list will never be empty, so you should stop waiting for it to be.

I hope you still call the people who matter most, even when it's inconvenient. Pick up the phone. Show up. Nobody remembers the perfect deadline, but they remember who was there.

I hope you've kept some curiosity alive, that you're still reading things that surprise you and still asking questions you can't answer yet. I hope you've changed your mind about something important, because that means you kept growing.

And I hope you're not chasing a version of success that looks good from the outside but feels hollow within. Measure your days by what you gave, what you learned, and whether you laughed.

Whatever you're doing now, I hope it's meaningful, and that you're at peace with the path that brought you there.

With hope,
Me, in 2026
